title: Two Stories about Flying (poems: How to Tell Wild Animals, The Ball Poem)

learn.hook: Every expert swimmer, flyer and speaker was once a beginner with shaking knees.
points: 'His First Flight' tells of a young seagull too afraid to fly; hunger finally pushes him off the ledge, and he discovers he can fly.
Reported (indirect) speech tells what someone said without quoting the exact words: He said that ...
When the reporting verb is in the past (said, told), tenses move one step back: is → was, can → could, will → would, has done → had done.
Pronouns change to fit the speaker: 'I' may become he or she.
Words of time and place change: now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, here → there, this → that.

example.q: Passage: Tara stood at the edge of the diving board in Pune. 'I can't do it,' she whispered. Her coach, Mr Rao, said, 'You can. I will be right here.' She shut her eyes, jumped, and came up laughing. Report Tara's words: 'I can't do it.'
steps: The reporting verb 'whispered' is in the past, so 'can't' becomes 'couldn't'.
'I' refers to Tara, so it becomes 'she'.
Add 'that' after the reporting verb.
example.answer: Tara whispered that she couldn't do it.

learn.reallife: News reports use reported speech all the time: 'The coach said that the team was ready.'

games.title: Tara's dive
games.prompt: Put the events of the passage in order
items: Tara stood at the edge of the board.
She whispered that she couldn't do it.
Her coach told her she could.
She shut her eyes and jumped.
She came up laughing.

quiz.q: In 'His First Flight', what finally makes the young seagull fly?
quiz.explain: He is starving, dives at the food his mother holds out, and finds himself flying.
steps: The young seagull was too afraid to fly and was left without food.
Starving, he dived at the fish his mother held out — hunger made him fly.
Answer: Hunger
quiz.mistake: Guesses a common cause instead of recalling the story

quiz.q: Passage: Tara stood at the edge of the diving board in Pune. 'I can't do it,' she whispered. Her coach, Mr Rao, said, 'You can. I will be right here.' She shut her eyes, jumped, and came up laughing. How did Tara feel before the jump?
quiz.explain: She whispered 'I can't do it', which shows fear.
steps: Tara whispered 'I can't do it' at the edge of the board.
That shows she was afraid.
Answer: Afraid
quiz.mistake: Reads only the happy ending

quiz.q: Change to reported speech: She said, 'I can't do it.'
options: She said that I can't do it.
She said that she can't did it.
She said that she couldn't do it.
She said that she won't do it.
quiz.explain: 'Can't' moves back to 'couldn't' and 'I' becomes 'she'.
steps: After 'said', 'can't' moves back to 'couldn't'.
'I' becomes 'she': She said that she couldn't do it.
Answer: She said that she couldn't do it.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to change the pronoun or the modal

quiz.q: Change to reported speech: Mr Rao said, 'I will be right here.'
options: Mr Rao said that I will be right here.
Mr Rao said that he will be right here.
Mr Rao said that he would be right here now.
Mr Rao said that he would be right there.
quiz.explain: 'Will' becomes 'would', 'I' becomes 'he', and 'here' becomes 'there'.
steps: After 'said', 'will' becomes 'would' and 'I' becomes 'he'.
'Here' changes to 'there' because the place has changed.
Answer: Mr Rao said that he would be right there.
quiz.mistake: Changes the tense but not the place word

quiz.q: In reported speech after 'said', 'today' usually becomes...
quiz.explain: 'Today' becomes 'that day' because the report is made at a later time.
steps: The report is made later, so 'today' is no longer today.
It becomes 'that day'.
Answer: that day
quiz.mistake: Thinks time words stay the same

quiz.q: Change to reported speech: Ravi said, 'I am learning to swim.'
options: Ravi said that he is learnt to swim.
Ravi said that he was learning to swim.
Ravi said that I was learning to swim.
Ravi said that he had learn to swim.
quiz.explain: Present continuous 'am learning' becomes past continuous 'was learning'.
steps: Present continuous 'am learning' moves back to past continuous 'was learning'.
'I' becomes 'he': Ravi said that he was learning to swim.
Answer: Ravi said that he was learning to swim.
quiz.mistake: Does not shift the present tense back to the past

quiz.q: Which word means the same as 'timid'?
quiz.explain: Timid means shy and easily frightened.
steps: Timid means shy and easily frightened.
So its synonym is fearful; bold and brave are opposites.
Answer: Fearful
quiz.mistake: Picks an antonym instead of a synonym

quiz.q: What is the opposite of 'courage'?
quiz.explain: Cowardice is lack of courage.
steps: Courage is bravery in the face of fear.
Its opposite is cowardice.
Answer: Cowardice
quiz.mistake: Chooses a word that means the same as courage

teach.ask: Gappu: My friend said, 'I can fly.' How do I tell Mummy what he said without using his exact words?
teach.praise: Flap-flap! 'He said that he could fly.' Tense steps back and 'I' becomes 'he'. I can report now!
teach.nudge: What happens to 'can' and to 'I' when you report someone's words?

revise.summary: In 'His First Flight', a young seagull too afraid to fly is pushed by hunger off the ledge and discovers he can fly. We also learn to change statements into reported speech.
focus: Recall that hunger finally makes the young seagull fly.
Change direct statements into reported speech after a past reporting verb.
Change pronouns and time/place words correctly.
remember: After a past reporting verb, tenses move one step back: is → was, can → could, will → would, has done → had done.
now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, here → there, this → that.
She said, 'I can't do it.' → She said that she couldn't do it.
traps: Don't forget to change the pronoun or the modal: 'I can't' → 'she couldn't'.
Don't change the tense but leave the place word: 'here' becomes 'there'.
Time words do not stay the same: 'today' becomes 'that day'.

learn.hook: A plane appears out of a storm, guides a lost pilot home, and then the control tower says no such plane was ever there.
points: 'The Black Aeroplane' is a mystery: a pilot lost in a storm follows a strange black aeroplane to safety, yet the control tower says no other plane was flying.
A mystery gives clues but leaves some questions unanswered, so readers keep guessing.
Modals of deduction show how sure we are: must = almost certain; can't = certain it is not true; may/might/could = possible.
For the past, add 'have' + past participle: 'Someone must have entered.' 'He can't have left.'
Other modals: should (advice), would (polite request), need not/needn't (no necessity).

example.q: Passage: At midnight, a soft tune drifted from the locked music room of the old Shimla guest house. In the morning, the caretaker, who kept the only key, found fresh rose petals on the piano keys. Using a modal, what can you say about the petals?
steps: The petals were fresh in the morning, so they were placed during the night.
Only the caretaker had the key; nobody else could easily enter.
We are almost sure someone was inside, though not who: use 'must have' for strong certainty.
example.answer: Someone must have been in the music room last night.

learn.reallife: Detectives, doctors and even weather forecasters use deduction: 'It might rain', 'He must have the flu', 'The thief can't have gone far.'

games.title: How sure is the speaker?
items: The lights are on; they must be home.
It can't be Ravi; he is in Delhi today.
That must be the postman at the door.
She may come tomorrow.
It might snow in Manali this week.
He could be at the library.

quiz.q: In 'The Black Aeroplane', what was strange about the plane that guided the pilot?
options: The control tower said no other plane was flying
It belonged to his own airline
quiz.explain: The woman in the control tower said his was the only plane she could see on the radar, so the guide plane remains a mystery.
steps: The pilot followed the black plane through the storm.
The control tower said his was the only plane on the radar — so no other plane was flying.
Answer: The control tower said no other plane was flying
quiz.mistake: Remembers that the plane was black but not why it was mysterious

quiz.q: Who tells the story in 'The Black Aeroplane'?
options: The woman in the control tower
The pilot of the black aeroplane
quiz.explain: It is a first-person story told by the pilot.
steps: The story is told in the first person ('I').
The narrator is the pilot of the Dakota.
Answer: The pilot of the Dakota
quiz.mistake: Confuses the narrator with another character

quiz.q: Passage: At midnight, a soft tune drifted from the locked music room of the old Shimla guest house. In the morning, the caretaker, who kept the only key, found fresh rose petals on the piano keys. Choose the modal: 'The petals were fresh, so someone ___ have been in the room at night.'
quiz.explain: Fresh petals are strong evidence, so 'must have' shows near certainty.
steps: Fresh petals are strong evidence of a recent visit.
Near certainty about the past = must have.
Answer: must
quiz.mistake: Picks a modal of advice or necessity instead of deduction

quiz.q: Choose the modal: 'The door was locked and the window was sealed, so the visitor ___ have left through them.'
quiz.explain: Both exits were closed, so it is impossible: 'can't have'.
steps: The door was locked and the window sealed.
Leaving through them was impossible: can't have.
Answer: can't
quiz.mistake: Does not see that the clues rule the possibility out

quiz.q: Choose the modal: 'Take an umbrella. It ___ rain later; the sky is getting cloudy.'
quiz.explain: Clouds make rain possible but not certain, so 'might' fits.
steps: Cloudy skies make rain possible, not certain.
Possibility = might.
Answer: might
quiz.mistake: Uses a past or negative modal for a future possibility

quiz.q: Which modal shows the strongest certainty?
quiz.explain: 'Must' in deduction means the speaker is almost sure.
steps: Might, may and could show possibility.
'Must' shows the strongest certainty.
Answer: must
quiz.mistake: Thinks all modals show the same level of certainty

quiz.q: What does 'mysterious' mean?
quiz.explain: Something mysterious puzzles us because we cannot explain it.
steps: Something mysterious puzzles us.
It is difficult to explain or understand.
Answer: Difficult to explain or understand
quiz.mistake: Links the word only to 'old' or 'spooky' places

quiz.q: Which word means 'completely puzzled'?
quiz.explain: Baffled means totally puzzled.
steps: Baffled means completely puzzled.
Delighted, relieved and tired mean other feelings.
Answer: Baffled
quiz.mistake: Confuses a feeling of puzzlement with other emotions

teach.ask: Gappu: My seeds vanished from my cup! Did a squirrel take them? How do I say I'm almost sure, or only guessing?
teach.praise: Peep! 'A squirrel must have taken them' if I see footprints, but 'might have' if I'm only guessing. Mystery solved!
teach.nudge: Which modal would you use when you are sure, and which when it is only possible?

revise.summary: 'The Black Aeroplane' is a mystery in which a pilot lost in a storm follows a strange black aeroplane to safety, though the control tower says no other plane was flying. We also use modals of deduction to show how sure we are.
focus: Explain why the black aeroplane is a mystery.
Choose must / can't / may / might / could from the clues given.
Use 'have' + past participle for deductions about the past.
remember: must = almost certain; can't = certain it is not true; may/might/could = possible.
Past deduction: 'Someone must have entered.' 'He can't have left.'
should (advice), would (polite request), need not/needn't (no necessity).
traps: Don't pick a modal of advice or necessity when the sentence needs deduction.
Don't use 'must have' when the clues rule something out; then it is 'can't have'.
The mystery is not that the plane was black but that the tower said no other plane was flying.

topics.title: Loss and growing up: tone in poems

learn.hook: Losing a favourite thing hurts. But what if that hurt is also a lesson?
points: 'The Ball Poem' by John Berryman shows a boy who loses his ball and, for the first time, learns what loss means.
The poet does not buy him another ball, because he wants the boy to learn to bear loss himself; that is part of growing up and taking responsibility.
'How to Tell Wild Animals' by Carolyn Wells is a humorous poem that 'teaches' readers to identify animals in a funny, exaggerated way.
Tone is the writer's attitude shown through words: humorous, serious, sad, hopeful, angry.
The same subject can have different tones: the loss of a ball is serious in Berryman; danger from wild animals is funny in Wells.

example.q: Poem: My kite snapped free above the Jaipur roofs / And drifted past the sun; / I cried, then learnt that some things go— / And growing up's begun. What is the tone of the last line, and what has the speaker learnt?
steps: The speaker first cries, so there is sadness.
Then the speaker 'learnt that some things go', which is acceptance.
'Growing up's begun' sounds calm and hopeful.
example.answer: The tone becomes accepting and hopeful; the speaker has learnt that some losses are part of growing up.

learn.reallife: Moving to a new city, a friend changing schools or a broken toy all teach us to accept loss and carry on.

games.title: Words for feelings
pairs: a duty to deal with something

games.title: Loss, humour and tone
items: 'The Ball Poem' was written by John Berryman.
John Berryman is the poet.
In 'The Ball Poem', the poet quickly buys the boy a new ball.
He chooses not to, so the boy can learn to bear loss.
'How to Tell Wild Animals' has a humorous tone.
It jokes about identifying animals in dangerous ways.
Tone is the number of lines in a poem.
Tone is the writer's attitude or feeling.
Learning to accept loss is part of growing up.
That is the main idea of 'The Ball Poem'.

quiz.q: Who wrote 'The Ball Poem'?
quiz.explain: John Berryman wrote 'The Ball Poem'.
steps: 'The Ball Poem' is in this chapter.
It was written by John Berryman.
Answer: John Berryman
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the two poems of this chapter

quiz.q: What does the boy in 'The Ball Poem' learn?
options: That loss is part of life and he must learn to bear it
How to swim in the harbour
That his friends will always replace his toys
quiz.explain: Losing the ball teaches him, for the first time, what loss means.
steps: The boy loses his ball and feels loss for the first time.
He learns that loss is part of life and he must learn to bear it.
Answer: That loss is part of life and he must learn to bear it
quiz.mistake: Takes the poem literally as being only about a toy

quiz.q: Why does the poet in 'The Ball Poem' not buy the boy another ball?
options: He is angry with the boy
He wants the boy to learn to accept loss himself
quiz.explain: Money can't replace what is lost; the boy must learn responsibility for his feelings.
steps: Buying a new ball would not teach him anything.
The poet wants the boy to learn to accept loss himself.
Answer: He wants the boy to learn to accept loss himself
quiz.mistake: Gives a practical reason that the poem does not suggest

quiz.q: Poem: My kite snapped free above the Jaipur roofs / And drifted past the sun; / I cried, then learnt that some things go— / And growing up's begun. What has the speaker learnt?
options: Some things are lost for good, and that is part of growing up
quiz.explain: The speaker says 'some things go' and 'growing up's begun'.
steps: The speaker says 'some things go' and 'growing up's begun'.
So: some things are lost for good, and that is part of growing up.
Answer: Some things are lost for good, and that is part of growing up
quiz.mistake: Picks a detail of setting instead of the lesson

quiz.q: Poem: My kite snapped free above the Jaipur roofs / And drifted past the sun; / I cried, then learnt that some things go— / And growing up's begun. What is the rhyme scheme?
quiz.explain: Only 'sun' and 'begun' (lines 2 and 4) rhyme.
steps: Line-endings: roofs (a), sun (b), go (c), begun (b).
Only lines 2 and 4 rhyme: abcb.
Answer: abcb
quiz.mistake: Assumes alternate lines always rhyme

quiz.q: What is the tone of 'How to Tell Wild Animals' by Carolyn Wells?
quiz.explain: It gives silly, exaggerated ways to identify animals, which makes it funny.
steps: The poem gives silly, exaggerated ways to identify animals.
That makes its tone humorous.
Answer: Humorous
quiz.mistake: Thinks a poem about wild animals must be frightening

quiz.q: What is 'tone' in a poem?
options: The writer's attitude or feeling shown through the words
quiz.explain: Tone tells us how the writer feels about the subject.
steps: Tone is how the writer feels about the subject.
It is shown through the choice of words.
Answer: The writer's attitude or feeling shown through the words
quiz.mistake: Confuses tone with structure or rhyme

quiz.q: Which word means the same as 'grief'?
quiz.explain: Grief and sorrow both mean deep sadness.
steps: Grief is deep sadness.
Its synonym is sorrow.
Answer: Sorrow
quiz.mistake: Picks an unrelated emotion

teach.ask: Gappu: I lost my favourite feather and I'm so sad. Why does the poet say losing things helps us grow up?
teach.praise: Sniff... chirp! Losing things teaches us to accept and carry on. I'm growing up!
teach.nudge: What does a loss teach us? Think about accepting it and growing up.

revise.summary: 'The Ball Poem' by John Berryman shows a boy learning what loss means, while 'How to Tell Wild Animals' by Carolyn Wells is humorous. Tone is the writer's attitude shown through words.
focus: Explain what the boy learns and why the poet does not buy him another ball.
Identify the tone of a poem: humorous, serious, sad, hopeful or angry.
Compare the tones of the two poems.
remember: Tone is the writer's attitude shown through words.
The poet wants the boy to learn to bear loss himself; that is part of growing up and taking responsibility.
'How to Tell Wild Animals' is humorous: it 'teaches' readers to identify animals in a funny, exaggerated way.
traps: Don't read 'The Ball Poem' as being only about a toy; it is about loss.
Don't think a poem about wild animals must be frightening; Wells's tone is humorous.
Tone is not the same as structure or rhyme.
